claims.text: Atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity induce local lattice distortions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Local lattice distortions create a rugged energy landscape.
The rugged energy landscape makes vacancy and self-interstitial mobilities more nearly equal.
More equal vacancy and interstitial mobilities enhance defect recombination.
Enhanced defect recombination limits irradiation-induced defect clusters such as dislocation loops.
Enhanced defect recombination suppresses precipitation caused by phase separation.
Suppressing defect clustering and precipitation stabilizes a single-phase microstructure.
The proposed mechanism preserves high-temperature strength.
The proposed mechanism preserves environmental resistance.
The proposed mechanism improves radiation tolerance.
The proposed mechanism preserves cryogenic toughness.
Slightly changing elemental proportions, including Al content, can systematically vary lattice distortion while retaining a single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy.
An optimized-distortion Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy will develop fewer irradiation-induced defects than a lower-distortion baseline.
An optimized-distortion alloy will minimize irradiation- or annealing-induced precipitate formation relative to the lower-distortion baseline.
An optimized-distortion alloy will retain superior mechanical properties relative to the lower-distortion baseline.
A lower atomic-size mismatch will produce less effective defect recombination and more defect clustering or precipitation.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions at irradiation doses up to about 8 dpa and thermal exposures up to 1073 K.
Severe cold working, contamination, grain-boundary character, or processing history may dominate or alter defect dynamics.
The quantitative relationship between lattice distortion and defect-recombination efficiency is not established.
